name: Cardiff Giant
hook: A carved gypsum figure buried on a New York farm in 1868, dug up in 1869 and shown as a petrified giant.
claim: Laborers digging a well on William Newell's farm near Cardiff, NY, uncovered a 10-foot stone figure in October 1869, shown as a petrified giant or ancient statue. Newell's relative George Hull (brother-in-law per White 1905; popularly cousin) had secretly carved and buried it there a year earlier.

claimed_age.label: No fixed figure; ancient statue or petrified giant
claimed_age.basis: No scientific age was measured. Early theories ranged from a statue carved two-three centuries earlier (Boynton, initially) to an antediluvian, Biblical-era giant (Tribble 2008; White 1905).

accepted_age.label: AD 1868: carved and secretly buried as a hoax
accepted_age.basis: Calendar date, not a lab-dated age: gypsum quarried and carved in 1868, buried on Newell's farm, and 'discovered' in October 1869. Consistent with Hull's confession and the traced Iowa quarry origin.

orthodoxy_at_claim.label: Human soft tissue does not petrify into stone, and no genuine giant-sized human remains were known; scientists mostly rejected literal petrification at once.

unambiguous_signal.note: Even sympathetic early examiners disagreed sharply on what it was: a fossilized man, a petrified Indian prophet, a Jesuit-era statue, or (later) a Phoenician idol with an inscription.

documented_context.note: Recovered by hired laborers digging a well on private land, with no archaeological oversight; the seemingly undisturbed find had itself been staged about a year earlier.

multiple_dating_methods.note: No scientific dating method was applied; antiquity rested only on individual examiners' visual and geological impressions of the gypsum surface.

multiple_labs.note: No laboratory analysis is recorded. Opinions came from individual naturalists (Hall, Wescott, Boynton) examining the statue directly, not from lab tests.

professional_recovery.note: Uncovered by hired farm laborers digging a well, not by trained excavators. The state geologist and other scientists only examined it after exhibition had begun.

peer_reviewed_report.note: Opinions on origin and age circulated as newspaper reports and private letters (e.g., to Scientific American), not as a peer-reviewed technical report.

material_accessible.note: The statue was exhibited to paying visitors from the first days, including scientists, journalists and skeptics such as Marsh and White.

independent_teams.note: Several naturalists (Hall, Wescott, Boynton, Marsh, White) examined the statue within weeks, but as individuals, not organized teams; verdicts split before resolving toward fraud.

proponent_stake.note: Hull spent heavily to manufacture the statue; Newell charged 50 cents admission, reportedly took in about $20,000, and remitted several thousand dollars to Hull.

objections.text: Othniel Marsh judged the statue recently made: brief burial would have obliterated tool marks and roughened its polished surfaces, yet both were still sharp, so 'the giant must have been very recently buried.'
objections.outcome_note: Confirmed by the traced Iowa gypsum origin and, eventually, Hull's own admission; every account since treats the statue as a hoax.

objections.text: Local residents recalled a secretive, heavily loaded wagon delivering a large crated object to the Cardiff area about a year before the 'discovery,' suggesting a staged burial rather than a chance find.
objections.outcome_note: Matches Hull's later confession and the traced 1868 purchase, quarrying and shipment of the gypsum block from Iowa.

objections.text: A visiting Fort Dodge, Iowa lawyer recognized the statue's material as matching an unusually large gypsum block quarried and shipped from Fort Dodge under secretive circumstances the previous year.
objections.outcome_note: The land lease, quarryman Michael Foley, and shipment were confirmed as the statue's true origin, corroborating Hull's eventual admission.

status_note: Universally treated as a fabricated statue, not a genuine ancient object. Marsh's on-site verdict, the traced Iowa gypsum origin, and Hull's own eventual admission are mutually consistent; no scholarly source since has argued otherwise.
what_settled_it: By late 1869, Othniel Marsh's on-site verdict that the tool marks and polish were too fresh for old burial matched the independently traced origin of the gypsum (quarried near Fort Dodge, Iowa, and carved in Chicago in 1868); Hull's own admission, which followed, confirmed both.

timeline.event: Hull has a gypsum block quarried in Iowa, carved in Chicago into a giant figure, and buried on relative William Newell's farm near Cardiff, NY.
Newell's laborers 'discover' the figure while digging a well; Newell tents it and charges 50 cents admission.
Examiners split: Boynton, Hall and Wescott argue for an ancient statue or petrified man; Marsh calls it 'a most decided humbug.'
Boynton reverses himself, concluding from further study that the statue was probably buried no more than about three years.
A Fort Dodge, Iowa lawyer recognizes the gypsum's likely source; the land lease and quarryman Michael Foley are traced.
Hull sells his interest for exhibition; P. T. Barnum, refused a purchase, has a rival copy made and shown as the 'real' giant.
After the Fort Dodge affidavits circulate and a rival 'Phoenician idol' theory is floated, Hull publicly admits he manufactured and buried the statue.

falsifier: This record would be wrong if Hull's confession and the Fort Dodge quarry trail were themselves shown to be fabricated, and independent physical testing instead matched the statue's material and burial context to a genuinely ancient, undisturbed origin.

sources.citation: Gallaher, R.A. (1921). The Cardiff Giant. The Palimpsest 2(9).
sources.note: Read in full (open PDF). Direct quotes from Marsh ('a most decided humbug'), Hall, Wescott and Boynton; describes the Fort Dodge/Iowa quarrying, Galusha Parsons's tip, and Hull's confession.
Crossref confirms author/year/DOI; publisher abstract read and consistent with S1, describing the case as an elaborate hoax with Biblical-history overtones. Full text not accessed (paywalled).

sources.citation: White, A.D. (1905). Autobiography of Andrew Dickson White, vol. 2, ch. LVI, 'The Cardiff Giant: A Chapter in the History of Human Folly, 1869-1870'. New York: The Century Co.
sources.note: Read via grep (Project Gutenberg #1370, text mirror). Confirms Marsh's tool-mark quote, Hull as Newell's 'brother-in-law', manufactured underside/pose evidence, and the 1870 pamphlet date (fn19).

sources.citation: Pettit, M. (2006). 'The Joy in Believing': The Cardiff Giant, Commercial Deceptions, and Styles of Observation in Gilded Age America. Isis 97(4): 659-677.
sources.note: Crossref metadata and abstract confirm a peer-reviewed historical analysis of the case's scientific, religious and market epistemologies. Full text not accessed (paywalled).

confidence_note: Corroborated by a contemporary critic's account (White 1905, read directly) and a 1921 history, plus a peer-reviewed analysis (Pettit 2006); no scholarly dissent exists on the hoax verdict.
corrections: The brief's 'exposed quickly' fits Marsh's verdict (6 weeks after the October 1869 find) but not public belief: S1 says the statue's fame 'continued' for months, with a Barnum copy and a 'Phoenician idol' theory preceding Hull's admission.

This record could not verify some frequently repeated popular details (e.g., the names of the Chicago carvers, an exact confession date) against a checked source within budget, so they are omitted rather than asserted.
notes: One of the most documented hoaxes in American archaeology; no serious source disputes the verdict. The statue's own 'age' evidence was manufactured: its underside was grooved to look water-worn and pitted to fake weathering, and its 'agonized' pose came from re-carving after the block was shortened in transit (S1; White 1905). Examiners disagreed on what they saw: Wescott reported no chisel marks; Marsh saw them clearly. Popular accounts give exact confession/court dates and named Chicago carvers; not independently checked, so omitted from formal fields. Scholarly treatment is thin but now includes a peer-reviewed article (Pettit 2006, Isis) besides Tribble's 2008 monograph.

open_issues: Hull's confession month/day is still unsourced; 1870 is inferred from the Fort Dodge pamphlet's imprint date (White 1905 fn19) and chapter ordering, not stated outright by any source read.
Dropped S3/S4 (unread SAGE encyclopedia entries) rather than completing their editor/publisher fields, since neither supported any claim and S1/S2/S5/S6 already exceed the minimum source count.
Did not verify S2's subtitle/publisher suggested in the review ('The Giant from Cardiff that Fooled America', Rowman & Littlefield); lookup.py's Crossref metadata does not surface them.
Left the fraud explanation inside `claim` alongside what was claimed, rather than moving it entirely to accepted_age/what_settled_it; both already state it, so this is redundancy, not an error.
Did not add Boynton to key_critics (he began as a proponent and only later reversed); his reversal is instead recorded in timeline.
